activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Mandarin Chinese, zuǒ means left and yòu means right, each said with its own tone.
story:
Jack sat in the school library with a folded map of a pretend Chinese town spread across the table. Ms. Romano had set up the exercise for the language club: ask for directions in Mandarin, then follow the answer to find the hidden paper star. Jack had one goal today, and it was not to end up in the pretend river again like last week.

"You went swimming twice," said Jewel, sliding into the chair across from him. "In a map."

"The river was invisible," Jack said. "That's my story and I'm keeping it."

He spread his flashcards and thought about his grandfather. Every summer visit, they walked to the market together, and his grandfather would point at corners and say the same two words over and over. "Zuǒ," he would say, pointing left, and then, turning his hand the other way, "yòu." Each word had its own tone, the way his grandfather said it, one dipping down, one falling like a dropped stone. Jack had repeated them at every intersection for three weeks, and by the end he could navigate the whole neighborhood without his grandfather pointing at all.

He tested the words now, tapping the map. "Zuǒ means left," he said, "and yòu means right. If I actually listen for the tone instead of panicking, I can tell them apart."

Heinrich arrived holding the answer sheet for the round, sworn to secrecy, and Jack asked his question: where was the star? Heinrich answered in Mandarin, rapid and flat, and Jack felt the panic rising, the same panic that had steered him into the river before. He made himself slow down. Two words kept recurring, and one of them dipped down, the way his grandfather's had at the corner by the noodle shop. Dipping meant left. Falling meant right.

"Left at the bridge, then right," Jack said, mostly to himself, and moved his finger along the map. "Twice right at the end, I think."

He traced the path and stopped on the square with the little drawn pavilion. "There."

Jewel leaned over. "You're sure? Because last time you were so sure that you drowned."

"I had a concussion of pride," Jack said. "Not permanent, though."

Heinrich turned over the sheet, and there it was, the pavilion square circled in red. Jack whooped so loudly that Ms. Romano appeared from behind the biography shelf with one eyebrow raised, and Jewel hurried to disclose the whole game before they got kicked out of the library for the second time that semester.

"Keep it down," Ms. Romano said, but she was smiling. "And Jack, next round, try asking me. I lived in Xi'an for two years."

Jack folded his map and grinned. "Zuǒ or yòu, Ms. Romano. I'm ready."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Megan had one goal for the school talent show audition: keep her juggling act a secret until she walked on stage. Three flaming pins, or at least three tennis balls painted to look like flaming pins, depending on how the paint dried.

She practiced behind the gym, where nobody went except the recycling bins. On Thursday she managed eleven catches in a row, a personal record. On Friday, Omar appeared at the corner of the building before she had even picked up the second ball.

"That's your talent?" he said. "Juggling?"

"How did you find me?"

He held up his phone. On the screen was a map of the school, with a little cartoon Megan standing behind the gym. "Snap Map," he said. "It shows your real-time location to your friends. Launched in 2017, I think. My cousin told me."

Megan stared at the little cartoon version of herself. It was wearing a tiny scarf, which she did not own. Otherwise it was uncomfortably accurate, right down to the corner of the building where the map said she was standing, because she was standing there.

"I never installed anything like that," she said.

"It comes with the app. You probably just tapped through it."

That afternoon in Ms. Nair's class, Megan found it in her settings, three menus deep, like something hoping not to be found. There was a list of everyone who could see her: Omar, Issa, and nineteen other names she recognized only vaguely. One was a kid from her old school in another town. She had not spoken to him in two years, and he could apparently watch her move around like weather.

She had an intuition that the little dot updated even when she wasn't posting anything, so she decided to test it. During lunch she left her phone with Issa, walked to the library, and came back. Issa showed her the screen. The dot had made the whole trip without her, faithfully strolling to the library and home again, like a dog that had learned the route.

"You walked past the library, though," Issa said. "You looped by the cafeteria."

"I did. And it saw that too."

After school, Megan turned the whole thing off. Then she went back behind the gym, where Omar was already leaning against the recycling bins, holding his phone up like a reporter.

"Took you long enough," he said. "Your dot's been standing at the flagpole for ten minutes."

"That's the point," Megan said. "The flagpole is where I leave it now." She picked up the first tennis ball, still slightly tacky from the paint.

Omar lowered the phone. "Eleven catches," he said. "You want to make it twelve before Friday?"

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
story:
Maya pressed her palms against the warm metal tray of soup and followed the line of steam down the counter. Why did the soup kitchen need so many volunteers on a school holiday in January? Her whole class had signed up, and Mr. Doyle had driven five of them over in his van, but nobody had explained why a day off became a day of work.

"You're new," said a woman behind the counter, handing Maya a ladle. "Scoop, pass, smile. That's the whole job."

Beside her, Cullen was already moving like he'd done this for years, sliding bread slices onto trays with meticulous care, straightening each one so the edges lined up. Maya watched a man in a gray coat take his bowl and cup his hands around it, breathing in the vapor before he ate, like the warm air itself was food.

Flashback: last January, Maya had been home on the same holiday, sleeping until ten, and she remembered seeing a news clip where people in orange vests painted a fence and picked up trash. She had wondered then why the reporters kept calling it a day of service. Now, ladling soup in a noisy room that smelled of onions and bleach, she turned the question over. It had to mean the holiday itself asked something of people. She remembered Mr. Doyle saying the word "King Holiday and Service Act" when he passed out permission slips. She tested her idea quietly, the way she tested things: "Cullen, is this why the whole school signs up? Because the holiday is a national day of volunteer service?"

"Since 1994," Cullen said, not looking up from the bread. "The King Holiday and Service Act was signed that year. Made the day into service. My sister's been coming every year since kindergarten."

Maya felt the pieces click. The act, the signing, the date: it was a rule she couldn't see, but she could see its results all around her, a room full of kids on a day off, scooping and passing and smiling.

At two o'clock the crowd thinned, and the woman behind the counter pointed to a stack of dented cans. "Salvage what you can," she said. "Dents are fine, bulges are not." Maya picked up a can and turned it over in her hands, checking the sides, wondering what else in this building had been rescued and given a second job.

Mr. Doyle leaned in the doorway. "Same time next January?"

Maya looked at the empty ladle in her hand. "Can we come in April too, when there's no holiday making us?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
story:
Anthony pressed his nose against the bookshop window, where a dusty sign said they planned to renovate the whole store next month. Inside, a shelf labeled CLASSICS had exactly one copy of The Most Dangerous Game left, and Jayla was reaching for it at the same time.

"I saw it first," Anthony said, grabbing the spine.

"Ms. Holloway needs it for our short story unit," Jayla said. "You can't even explain foreshadowing. That's the whole quiz on Friday."

"Can too." Anthony flipped the book open right there between the shelves. His eyes caught the first page. "Wait. The sailors call it Ship-Trap Island. They're scared of the place, even from far away."

Jayla peered over his shoulder. "It's just a name."

"Names mean stuff, though." Anthony tapped the page. "Ship-Trap. Like the island is a trap made of... ships? Or for ships?" He dug in his backpack and pulled out his notebook. His class had a running list called "sneaky clues," and so far it only had three sad entries from a story about a dog that turned out not to be dangerous at all. He wrote: sailors fear the island before anything happens. It's a warning.

Poppy appeared from the graphic novel section, carrying a book about raccoons. "Ooh, are you being a scavenger for clues? Because I found a raccoon that steals pens."

"Look," Anthony said, and read the opening aloud in his best dramatic voice. A yacht, a dark night, and sailors who felt dread at the mere mention of the island's name. "So if the story is called The Most Dangerous Game, and there's a hunter on board who keeps talking about hunting, then the fear of that island has to hint at danger waiting there."

Jayla frowned. "Hint. Foreshadow. You're doing it."

"I'm doing it." Anthony grinned so wide his cheeks hurt.

They bought the book between the three of them, each paying an approximate third of the price, and Poply threw in an extra nickel so nobody had to wait for change. Outside, the afternoon sun made the sidewalk glow. Jayla held up her palm for a high five, then stopped.

"You still have to explain symbolism," she said. "By Friday."

Anthony looked down at the cover, where the island's dark shape loomed behind the title like something waiting. "The island is a trap," he said slowly. "Maybe the whole island means something. Maybe it's a symbol."

Jayla's hand was still hanging in the air.

"Don't leave me hanging," Anthony said, and slapped it.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: Buying a fund that holds many different stocks, called diversifying, means one company's collapse hurts much less than if all the money were in that one stock.
story:
Beatrice stood in line at the bank beside her mother, holding a page of homework questions so tightly the paper creased. Question three read: "Which is riskier, a stock or a bond, and why?" She was supposed to interview someone at the bank, but now that she was actually here, her mouth felt dry.

Behind her, two voices were arguing. Beatrice turned and recognized Kiara and Isha from her grade, waiting with a parent of their own.

"It's not fair," Kiara was saying. "My dad put all his money in one company, and the company crashed. He lost basically everything." Her chin wobbled a little, and Isha patted her arm.

"That's the weird part," Isha said. "My grandma had money in that same company too, but hers was inside a fund that holds a whole bunch of different stocks. When the company crashed, she only lost a little."

Beatrice forgot about her dry mouth. "Wait," she said. "Same company, same crash, totally different results?"

"That's what I keep trying to figure out," Kiara said. "I keep imagining it like dominoes. One falls, they all fall."

Isha shook her head. "It's more like the fund spread the dominoes out. That's called diversifying," she said. "Grandma says it means holding many different stocks, so one company going under hurts a lot less than if all the money were in that one stock."

"That's the word my mom uses!" Beatrice flipped her page over and wrote diversifying in big letters, then drew a circle around it. "Okay, so a bond is a promise to pay you back, like a loan. A stock is owning a tiny piece of a company. If the company dies, your piece dies with it. Like, extinct." She tapped her pencil. "So a single stock is riskier, because everything depends on one company surviving."

A woman in a navy blazer opened the counter beside the teller windows. "Beatrice? I'm Ms. Haddad. Your mother said you had questions for a school project." She smiled at all three girls. "Do your friends want to sit in too?"

They trooped after her to a small desk with a bowl of peppermints. Before any question could precede Beatrice's own careful opening line, Kiara blurted, "Is my dad bad with money?"

Ms. Haddad considered this through the lens of long experience, or so it seemed to Beatrice, because she answered slowly and kindly. "No. He put his faith in one thing, and one thing let him down. Plenty of careful people have done the same."

"Then he could put some money in a fund," Isha said. "Like my grandma."

"He says funds are boring," Kiara admitted, but she was digging in her backpack for a pen, and she copied Beatrice's circled word onto her hand.

"Boring survives crashes," Beatrice said, and slid her homework across the desk. "Ms. Haddad, can I write down that bonds are promises and stocks are pieces of companies, and the riskiest thing of all is one single stock with nothing else around it?"

"You may," said Ms. Haddad, dropping three peppermints into their hands. "And tell your teacher the example you found standing in line."

Kiara looked at the word inked on her palm and grinned. "I'm showing my dad tonight."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well, a condition called presbyopia that reading glasses correct.
story:
Grandpa had been in the backyard for ten minutes, holding the tomato seed packet at arm's length and squinting at it like it was a distant hawk. Raphael watched him from the porch, chewing the last of his toast. At the market cafe on Saturday, Grandpa had done the same thing with the menu, stretching his arm out until Raphael finally read the specials out loud for him. Two times was a coincidence, maybe. Three would be a pattern. He wiped his hands on his jeans and went down the steps.

"Grandpa, can you read this?" Raphael held up the watering schedule he'd written, first close to his grandfather's face, then slowly pulling it back the length of his arm. Grandpa blinked at it, frowned, blinked again.

"Stop waving it around like a flag, kiddo. Bring it back a bit." At about arm's length, Grandpa nodded. "There. Whoever heard of a boy writing so small anyway." Raphael inhaled the smell of turned earth and mulch and said nothing, but he marked the distance on the schedule with his thumbnail. It was the same distance as the menu, the same as the seed packet. Whatever was going on, it lived in his grandfather's eyes, and it lived at exactly that range.

Luis came over after lunch, drawn by the promise of the old treehouse ladder, but Raphael showed him the schedule first and explained his test. "So near is blurry and far is fine," Luis said, turning the paper over. "My mom does the same arm thing with her phone." Grandpa, who had been listening from the tomato bed, sat back on his heels and laughed.

"It's called presbyopia," he said. "After about forty, the lens of the eye loses flexibility, and it can't focus up close the way it used to. Reading glasses fix it. I've got a pair somewhere in my suitcase, if I ever unpack it." He brushed dirt off his knees. Raphael remembered being impulsive last summer, laughing when his other grandpa held a birthday card out like that, and how quickly the laughing had stopped when nobody else joined in. He hadn't thought about that in a year, and now here he was, catching the same thing before anyone could tease anybody.

Grandpa never did find the glasses that week, but Raphael left the watering schedule pinned to the shed door in oversized letters, every word big enough to read from across the yard. On Thursday morning Grandpa stood in front of it, hands on hips, and read the whole thing out loud from the picnic table.

"Look at that," he said. "The scavenger who planted these tomatoes also wrote me the only sign in town I can see."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The community centre was holding its first Heritage Night, and Romy had signed up to build the welcome display. She was gluing a balsa-wood model airplane above the sign-in table when Timothy and Philip started arguing beside her, loud enough that she could hear them over the hum of the folding chairs being dragged into place.

"You can't be in the Métis group," Philip was saying. "Your dad isn't Métis. Only your grandma is, and she's not even here tonight."

"My mom says I'm Métis," Timothy said. "She says we're all registered through the nation, and that's that."

"That's not how it works. You have to look the part. You have to be, like, fully from that group."

Romy turned the model over in her hands, checking the propeller she had carved from a coffee stir stick. The blades were set at an angle so they would actually spin. She found herself wondering what rule, if any, decided a question like theirs. You couldn't see belonging the way you could see a propeller or a uniform. Maybe, she thought, there was a written answer somewhere, the way there was a written angle for the blades.

"Ms. Nolan," she called, "is there a computer I can use for ten minutes?"

The activity room had two old laptops. Romy typed in her question about who decides what group a person belongs to. The answer came up faster than she expected. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership. She read the line twice. It meant Timothy's nation decided Timothy's membership, not Philip. She could deduce that from the wording alone, and she wanted to test it before she trusted it.

Back in the gym, she found Timothy alone by the juice table. She showed him the screen. "It's the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples," she said. "Adopted 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

Timothy read it slowly, and his shoulders came up from where they had been sagging. "So Philip doesn't get a vote."

"Nobody outside your nation does, by the sound of it."

Philip appeared with a paper plate of samosas, because his own family was presenting the food table and he wanted, more than anything tonight, to be the one who knew the most in the room. He read the declaration over Timothy's shoulder, and his face went through several expressions before settling on grudging respect. "Fine. But you still have to come see our table. My grandmother made three kinds, and I helped with two."

By the end of the evening, the gym smelled like frybread and curry, and someone's grandfather was playing fiddle near the stage. Timothy had pinned a small beaded pin to his jacket, one his grandmother had sent. Romy gave the model airplane one last look, flicked the propeller with her finger, and watched it spin.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
Sawyer had one job until noon, when the toddler's mother got back from her interview, and that job was sitting on a bench at Riverside Park watching her son push a plastic duck around the edge of the splash pond. The pond was barely a puddle, two inches deep at the most, so at first it had seemed safe to glance at his phone. Then he remembered the line from the babysitting card his aunt had given him, and he stopped glancing.

Matthias arrived at ten, carrying a remote-control sailboat. "This is a descendant of the one my grandfather built," he said, holding it out. "His sank in 1989. This one won't." He crouched at the pond's far side to launch it, and Denise came jogging behind him with a towel, already arguing that the pond was too small for a real race.

The toddler took one look at the sailboat and plunged his arms in after it, laughing. Sawyer scooped him up, dripping. "You have to hold him back," Denise said. "It's two inches of water. He's fine alone for a minute." It sounded naive to Sawyer, the way his own thinking had been naive an hour ago, before he'd really read the card. "Kids can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out," he said. "You can't ever leave them alone near a bath, or anything like one." Denise blinked at him, then at the pond, and didn't argue again.

Then Sawyer's phone rang, and the screen said it was the toddler's mother. Matthias waved him toward the quieter grass, so Sawyer did what the card had drilled: he wrapped the toddler in Denise's towel and carried him along, phone to one ear, wet boy on his hip. He didn't leave him by the water, not even for the length of a call. The interview had moved up, his mother said; she'd be there in ten minutes, not at noon.

Ten minutes. Matthias wanted his race before the sprinklers came on at eleven, because the schedule sheet taped to the pavilion post said the pond drained then, and a drained pond would end everything. So they raced with the toddler on Sawyer's hip, shrieking with delight every time the sail heeled over, Denise running alongside as the official judge even though she'd said the whole thing was silly. The boat crossed the reed they'd stuck in the mud as a finish line a full boat-length ahead of nothing, since it was the only boat, and Matthias raised both fists anyway.

When the toddler's mother hurried up the path, Sawyer handed over a damp, happy boy and a soggy plastic duck. "He never left the water alone," Denise announced before Sawyer could speak. "Not even for a phone call." Behind them, the sprinkler timer clicked, and the pond began to empty.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
story:
Rachel had a plan for Saturday morning, and the plan was this: she would do laundry so well that her mother would have to let her do it forever, which meant she would never again wash a single dish. She dragged the hamper into the kitchen, tipped it onto the tiles, and sorted the pile into hills. Dark hill, light hill, towel hill, and a small suspicious hill of things that had once been white but were now the colour of weak tea.

She was patting herself on the back, mentally, when Ophelia arrived in sock feet, holding her phone like a clipboard. "Bryan says you're doing laundry," Ophelia said. "He wants to know if you'll do his too." Rachel said that was a hypothetical question with a very firm answer, which was no. Then Ophelia picked up a cream sweater with wooden buttons from the top of the pile. It was hand-knitted, with a tag sewn inside in her grandmother's looping handwriting. Rachel assumed her mother had left it out for the next wash, since it smelled like campfire and old perfume.

They loaded the machine, poured in the detergent, and Rachel turned the dial to hot, because hot water seemed like the serious, professional choice. The drum thumped. They ate toast at the counter while the machine sloshed and groaned like a stomach ache. When it clicked off, Rachel pulled out the clothes one armful at a time: dark hill, light hill, towels, and then something that made her stop.

The sweater had become small enough for a doll. The sleeves were the length of mittens. Ophelia held it up with two fingers, and the wooden buttons hung on it like coins on a vest. Rachel turned the tag over, and under her grandmother's name, in smaller loops, were the words "WOOL. COLD ONLY." She had washed a wool sweater in hot, sloshing water, and it had shrunk.

"That's called felting," said Ophelia, who was reading from her phone. Rachel frowned and looked at the sweater again, at how tight and stiff the knitting had gone, almost like fabric instead of loops. So something had happened inside the wool itself, something she couldn't see, some invisible thing about the fibres that hot water and sloshing had set off. She narrowed her eyes at the machine as if it had done it on purpose.

She texted her mother a photograph of the tiny sweater, then flattened the rest of the laundry on the kitchen table and started folding towels, since towels could not betray her. Bryan texted back first: HA. Then her mother texted: We'll talk. Ophelia put the little sweater on a jam jar, where it fit perfectly, sleeves dangling like a cardigan for a very small librarian.

"We could say it's a memoir," Rachel said. "Grandma's sweater, in its second life."

"It's a doll sweater now," said Ophelia, and buttoned the top button.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: Defenders can answer a pick by switching, meaning the two defenders trade the players they are guarding.
story:
The hockey rink was empty of ice all summer, so Ms. Eze ran a three-on-three basketball clinic on the concrete floor where the zamboni usually parked. Ryan had signed up because he wanted to be a point guard, the one who decided where the ball went. So far he mostly dribbled in circles and hoped.

"Point guards talk," Ms. Eze said on the first Thursday. "If you don't call the play, you're just a kid with a ball." She showed them a pick and roll: one player stands in the defender's path, the ball handler uses that screen, and the screener then slips toward the hoop. Ryan practiced it with Nyla and Maelys until the lights buzzed overhead.

The landlord of the building had left the big garage doors open, and warm air rolled in from the parking lot. On Saturday the older kids showed up, including a tall boy named Devon, and they ran a real game, shirts against skins. Ryan took the point for his team.

He called the play. "Red, Red." Nyla came and set the screen on his defender, and Ryan drove around it, expecting a clear lane. Instead Devon stepped out in front of him. Devon had been guarding Maelys under the hoop, and now Devon was on Ryan. Ryan pulled the ball back out before he lost it, confused. His own defender was trailing somewhere behind the screen, chasing Maelys, who had wandered toward the basket with nobody on her.

At the next whistle he stood at the top and thought it through. It wasn't that his defender had gotten lost. The two defenders had traded who they were guarding. That was the answer to a pick, and it meant the big defender came to the ball. He wanted to test the idea before he trusted it.

"Maelys," he said quietly, "next possession, go set the screen yourself, then roll." He told Nyla to stay wide where her defender would have to choose. Then, to make sure Devon committed, Ryan simulated a hard drive, jabbing his foot toward the paint. Devon moved with him. Maelys screened Ryan's man and cut to the hoop, and the defender who had been guarding Maelys now chased Ryan around the screen. The trade had happened again, exactly as Ryan had guessed, which meant Maelys was open with a smaller player on her.

He fired the pass over Devon's outstretched arm. Maelys caught it, took one dribble, and laid it in off the backboard. Devon called for the ball on the other end, annoyed, and announced that nobody was immune to a good pump fake, which was not at all the same thing, but Ryan let him have it.

"Same play again," Ryan said, backing out to the top. He clapped once and put the ball above his head. "Red, Red."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
Andrew sat cross-legged on his grandfather's porch with a folded sheet of Arabic in his hands, mouthing the same line for the ninth time. The ceremony was in three weeks, and he was supposed to recite Surah Al-Fatiha by heart in front of the whole family. So far his tongue kept tripping over one word, and every trip made him laugh, which made him forget even more.

"That word," said his cousin Ravi from the rocking chair, "you're bending it like it's made of rubber. It's not rubber. It's more like cartilage. Firm but flexible."

"You're supposed to be helping, not doing anatomy class," Andrew said. Ravi was twenty, visiting for the summer, and had a habit of turning everything into a metaphor.

"Fine. Say it for me."

Andrew said the whole opening, got through the stubborn word, then blanked completely on the last line. He stared at the porch boards as if the answer might be knotted into the wood grain. "This is impossible. How does anybody memorize anything longer than this?"

Ravi set down his tea. "Recite chapter 36."

"What?"

"Just listen." And then Ravi began, his voice low and steady, verse after verse after verse, rolling out without a single pause or a single page. Andrew slid off the chair and stared. When Ravi finally stopped, ten minutes later, he grinned. "That's one chapter out of the whole Quran. All 114 chapters, and I know every one."

"From memory? All of it?" Andrew's voice cracked on "all," which was embarrassing, so he pretended a bug had flown into his mouth.

"There's a word for someone who's done it," Ravi said. "A hafiz."

Andrew tested something. "Okay, but you finished it once, so it's done, right? Like a video game. You beat it, you close the file."

Ravi laughed so hard the rocking chair squeaked. "Try me tomorrow. Ask me the same chapter again."

The next morning Andrew woke up early and found Ravi on the porch already reciting, eyes closed, fingers tapping his knee. He'd clearly been at it for a while. Andrew flopped into the other chair with his cereal and interrupted at chapter 36, and Rai picked it up mid-verse without blinking. Then Ravi kept going into another chapter entirely, and Andrew realized his cousin did this every single day, the way their grandfather watered the tomatoes every single day whether they looked thirsty or not. The memorizing wasn't a wall you built once. It was a living thing you fed.

"So it's never finished," Andrew said slowly. "Ever?"

"Ever," said Ravi. "Keeping it perfectly takes constant practice. Now stop looking so tragic and give me the Fatiha. And Andrew, if you crack up at that word again, I'm telling Tina you cried over a prayer."

"You wouldn't."

"Recite it properly and we'll never know."

Andrew straightened his back, took a breath that made his ribs creak, and began. The stubborn word came out firm but flexible, exactly like cartilage, and he kept going, one line, then the next, the morning sun beginning to radiate off the watering can by the tomatoes. When he finished the last verse without a single stumble, he opened his eyes and found Ravi holding up one finger.

"Chapter 36. First line. Go."

"Hey, I'm not the hafiz here."

"Not yet," Ravi said. "Porch. Same time tomorrow. Bring the cereal."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
Carson pushed his noodles around the plate while his phone buzzed for the third time. Maely had texted again: "Club votes Thursday. You're the tiebreaker. Pick a side."

"Everything all right?" his mother asked.

"The robotics club might split in two." He set the phone face down. "Here's what happened. At the regional meet, Tariq's robot malfunctioned, and he blamed a dead battery. That was a lie. The real reason was that he'd stayed up reprogramming it to cover for Gemma, who'd broken a part and asked him not to say anything. Mr. Visser found out last week."

"So he lied," his mother said.

"He covered for a friend," his father said, not looking up from his plate. "That's different."

"No, it isn't. He lied to a judge." Carson pulled out a sheet of notebook paper where he'd listed the facts. Everyone in the club agreed on all of them. Gemma broke the part. Tariq knew and said nothing. He blamed the battery. The team got a score it shouldn't have. Mr. Visser found out and disqualified them. Nobody disputed a single fact, and yet half the club thought Tariq did the right thing and half thought he betrayed the team. That was the part eating at him. He'd assumed that if people had the same facts, they'd land in the same place, and this was like discovering the sun didn't always rise.

"Both halves know exactly what happened," he said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Same facts. Different answer. So the fight isn't about facts at all. It's about what they value. Maely keeps saying the rules have to apply to everyone or the whole competition is meaningless. Gemma says Tariq was loyal, and you don't sell out a friend." He paused. "They're both valuing something real. Maely values fairness. Gemma values loyalty."

His mother raised an eyebrow. "And you?"

"That's what I have to figure out by Thursday." He told them the club had drafted a kind of contract at the start of the year, promising honesty at competitions, and everyone had signed it, including Tariq. His father argued that a promise to a friend outweighed a piece of paper, and his mother argued the opposite just as firmly, and Carson watched two people who agreed on every fact walk away in opposite directions. Then his phone buzzed again. Gemma: "You're not going to rat out the club at dinner, right?"

He typed back, "Tell Maely I have a proposal for Thursday. Nobody splits. We give back the score ourselves, before anyone makes us. And Tariq apologizes to Mr. Visser without naming who he protected." It wasn't a perfect fix. Someone would still be angry. But if the fight wasn't about facts, then arguing facts forever was pointless, and maybe the only move left was to give both sides something.

He set the phone down and picked up his fork. His mother slid the bread basket toward him, and his father, after a long moment, nodded. "That's fair," his father said. "And loyal, too."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Henry's problem was simple: Mr. Ramírez wanted a science fair project by Friday, and all Henry had was a dying bean plant on his windowsill and two weeks of nothing. Then Kane came over after school, saw the plant, and asked why it looked so sad.

"Maybe it's bored," Kane said. "My mom plays music for her ferns and they're vigorous. Huge. Practually jungle ferns."

Griffin, who had followed Kane in, shook his head. "That's not a thing."

"It could be a thing," Henry said, and he felt the project forming right there. He took a census of every bean seed in Mr. Ramírez's classroom drawer, twenty-four seeds, and set up six cups of soil with music playing beside them and six cups in silence. Each cup got the same water, the same spot on the counter near the window. "If music matters, the music cups should grow taller. If it doesn't, they'll come out about the same."

Mr. Ramírez walked past the counter on Monday and tapped one of the cups. "Before you go further," he said, "write down what 'no effect' would look like. Then you're testing something." He moved on to unjam the pencil sharpener, which had eaten a crayon again.

Henry stared at the empty line in his notebook. Griffin leaned over. "He means like, if the music does nothing, what happens?"

"Then there's no relationship between music and growth," Henry said slowly. "Same height either way. And the whole point of the experiment is to knock that idea over, to reject it. Like proving it wrong."

"It has a name, actually," Griffin said. "My sister calls it the null hypothesis. It's the statement that there is no relationship between the things you're studying, and your experiment tries to reject it." He paused. "I think that makes us scientists. Or at least people with dirt under their nails."

For ten days Henry measured sprouts with a ruler, recorded heights in milliliters of growth, which he then crossed out because milliliters were for liquid, and rewrote in centimeters. He made Kane stop humming near the control cups after Kane admitted he'd been doing it "for moral support." On day eleven, the music cups averaged 9 centimeters and the silent cups averaged 8.7. Henry looked at the numbers for a long time.

"So do we reject it?" Kane asked.

"Not really. That's basically the same." Henry taped the last measurement into his notebook: 8.7, 9, 8.7, 9. "The music didn't matter. But now we know, and nobody can say we guessed."

"Then I'm never playing the ferns another note," Kane said. "Think of the electricity we'll cease wasting."

"Your mom plays music for plants because she likes the music," Griffin said.

Kane considered this. "Yeah, all right. Hypothesis number two: my mom is the actual scientist."

Henry laughed so hard he knocked over cup eleven. He caught it before the soil hit the floor, and the sprout, silent all its life, kept right on standing.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
story:
The note was folded into a tight square and tucked into the side pocket of Adam's backpack, where Max had slipped it during math without saying a word. Adam waited until the group stopped for water, a mile up the trail, before he opened it. "Ask Mr. Hassan to borrow the orange," Max had written. "Willyam already knows. Do not lose this note." Below that, Willyam had added, in handwriting that leaned like it was in a wind, "It's about the science test."

Mr. Hassan was already holding the orange when Adam caught up to him at the overlook, which felt like a trick, though it was probably just that Mr. Hassan liked oranges. "Your classmate failed to explain the seasons on Friday," Mr. Hassan said. "Today you get one more chance before I authorize the retake. Walk with me."

"I know it's about the tilt," Adam said. "I just can't make it make sense."

"That is the whole problem with science," said Mr. Hassan. He handed Adam the orange and his small flashlight. "Make it make sense to us. Right here. If you can explain it on a mountain, you can explain it in a classroom."

Willyam grabbed a sharp twig and pushed it through the orange, straight through from top to bottom. "Axis," he announced, as if he had invented it. Max held the flashlight, standing in for the sun, and shined it while Adam tilted the twigged orange toward the light. One hemisphere glowed bright and direct; the other sat dimmer in the slanted beam.

"Summer up here," Adam said slowly, tipping the top toward Max's flashlight, "and winter down there. Same sunlight. Different angle." He kept the tilt, which was the hard part, and walked the orange around Max in a slow circle. "And it stays tilted the same way the whole way around, so the bright part switches sides halfway through." His heart was going fast. It was working.

Then Willyam said, "Let me try," and took the orange, and held the twig perfectly upright, straight up and down, like a flagpole. He orbited Max with it. Adam watched the lit side of the orange, waiting for the bright patch to slide toward the twig's top the way it had before. It didn't move. It just sat there, in the same spot, the same size, lap after lap around Max.

"Willyam," Adam said, "you broke it."

"I didn't touch anything!"

"You held it straight up. With no tilt, the light hits the same spot at the same angle the whole year. There's nothing to switch. There wouldn't be seasons at all. It would just be the same forever." Adam took the orange back and tipped it again, and there was summer, right where it was supposed to be. Somewhere below them a hawk turned in the warm air, riding the heat the way hawks do.

Mr. Hassan peeled an actual orange from his other pocket and ate it, watching. "Mr. Hassan," Adam said, "can the retake be up here? The curriculum is better on this trail."

"The curriculum," said Mr. Hassan, spitting a seed off the edge, "is wherever you figure things out." Max wrote one more note and handed it over: "You still owe me a flashlight battery, and that's not corrosive, that's a fact."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
story:
Brielle spotted the white tent from the far side of the park, its fabric so translucent that the morning sun shone right through it, glowing like a paper lantern. The whole gurdwara community had moved its celebration outdoors today, and the tent would serve as the prayer space.

"Wait," Dexter said, stopping at the tent flap. "I've never been to anything like this. Am I supposed to do something?"

"You have to take your shoes off first," Brielle said. She knelt and untied her sneakers. "Everyone does. It's like that at mosques and Hindu temples too. My cousin got married at a mandir last spring, and there was a whole shelf of shoes outside, hundreds of them, all mixed up."

Dexter pulled off his sandals, then hesitated, running a hand through his hair. "What about this? Is a hat okay?"

"You need something on your head in a gurdwara. A hat would work, but..." Brielle dug into her backpack and pulled out a folded scarf, bright orange with a thin silver border. "Here. I brought two on purpose."

"You planned this," Dexter said, but he was already twisting it into place, and it sat crooked over one ear.

"I planned it after last time," Brielle admitted. She adjusted his scarf, tucking the loose end so it lay flat. A year ago, before her friend Angela's family had taken her to the gurdwara on Marshall Street, Brielle had marched up the steps in sneakers with the laces still double-knot-hog-tied tight. Angela's grandmother had gently pointed at the shoe rack, and Brielle had spent four embarrassing minutes hopping on one foot while a line of patient people waited behind her. That day she had also turned up bareheaded, and a kind stranger had lent her a thin cotton square that kept sliding off. She'd spent the whole visit learning to interpret the small signals around her: when people bowed, when they sat, when the singing swelled and everyone pressed their palms together. By the end she'd understood that the rules weren't traps for newcomers. They were just things you could know ahead of time, if someone told you or if you watched.

Inside the tent, the ceiling fan turned in slow circles overhead, each revolution stirring the smell of cardamom from the steel pots where volunteers were stirring halva. An uncle nodded at Dexter's scarf and gave Brielle a thumbs up. They found a spot on the carpet beside Angela, who was already sitting cross-legged with her eyes half closed.

"Nice scarf," Angela whispered.

"Brought a spare," Brielle whispered back. "Rule number one of bringing your friend places: carry a backup."

The singers started, and the tabla player's hands blurred, and Dexter leaned over to whisper, "Okay, this is actually amazing," just as the fan swept another warm breath of cardamom down over all three of them.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
story:
The food bank shared its parking lot with the neighborhood cleanup, so Emily kept hearing the scrape of rakes and the crash of trash bags while she stood in the cool basement sorting canned beans. She had signed up because Catherine and Japji both claimed it would be fun, though so far the fun consisted of dust, the sour smell of cardboard, and an old sticker on her sleeve that said VOLUNTEER in peeling letters.

Mr. Oyelaran handed her a crate of newly donated corn. "Shelf four, please," he said, and hurried off to diagnose a strange clattering in the ceiling that he suspected was a rodent, possibly the same one that had chewed a box of oatmeal last spring. Emily lugged the crate over. The shelf already held corn, maybe twenty cans in a neat row, so she slid the new ones in front where they would look orderly and full.

When Mr. Oyelaran came back down, he studied the shelf and shook his head. "Redo it, please. New cans go behind." He said it kindly, but Emily's face went hot. Behind? That made the shelf look messy, with the older cans, some dented and dusty, blocking the bright new ones. She was still grumbling inside when Japji appeared with another crate. "He told me the same thing," Japji whispered. "I asked why, and he just said, 'first in, first out.' He's very proud of that phrase."

Emily stood in front of the shelf and turned the words over. First in, first out. The old cans had arrived first, so they left first. If she hid them behind the new ones, nobody would grab them until later, and cans had dates stamped on their lids, dates that did not care about looking orderly. She tested it, moving one dusty can to the front and reading its date aloud to herself, then a new one from the back for comparison. The old one was a year closer to its end. It was like the corn was standing in a line for checkout, and she had been cutting in front of the people who had waited longest.

"I get it," she told Mr. Oyelaran when he passed. "The old cans are endangered. If they hide back there, they'll expire before anyone takes them home." He laughed so hard the clipboard rattled. "Endangered corn. I like that." Upstairs, someone from the cleanup banged on the door, dropping off a bin of donated soup they had collected house to house, and Catherine shouted down the stairs that the rodent in the ceiling was actually just a squirrel, which everyone agreed was only slightly better.

Emily took the soup crate to shelf two, slid the new cans carefully behind the old ones, and straightened the row so the earliest dates stood first in line, right where hands would reach.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The saying that compound interest is 'the eighth wonder of the world' is often credited to Albert Einstein, but there is no reliable evidence he ever said it.
story:
Arianna had exactly one slide left to fix before math class, and it was the quote at the top: "Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world," attributed to Albert Einstein. She had written it in big letters because it made her poster about savings accounts sound important. But something about it nagged at her, the way a pebble in a shoe nags all the way home.

She found Salma at the lunch table, elbow-deep in a bag of chips. "You know that Einstein quote, the eighth wonder thing? Where did he say it?"

Salma shrugged. "Somewhere smart, probably. A lab. A blackboard place."

"That's not a source, that's a vibe." Arianna pulled out the library tablet and typed the quote in. The first result repeated the saying, but it also mentioned something else: there was no reliable evidence Einstein ever said it. She read the line twice. "It's a fake quote. It's everywhere, and it's fake."

"So you have to cut it from your poster?" Ellie slid into the seat across from them, stealing a chip. "Tragic. Your poster had one celebrity and now it has zero."

"I have to cut it or say what's true. I can't just repeat something nobody can trace back." Arianna tapped the table. "You know what's annoying? The saying still makes a point. Compound interest really does grow faster than simple interest. It just doesn't need a famous dead scientist to vouch for it."

In Ms. Friedman's class, after lunch, they were comparing the two kinds of interest over five years, the exact project on Arianna's poster. Ms. Friedman drew two lines on the board: one straight like a ruler, one that bent upward, curving away from the first like it was escaping. "Somebody give me one difference between them."

"With simple interest, you earn on the money you put in," Arianna said. "With compound, you earn on the money you put in plus the interest you already earned. The two lines look similar at first, then the gap gets bigger every year."

"Good. That's a distinct pattern, not just a bigger number." Ms. Friedman capped her marker. "Arianna, you look like you're about to burst."

Arianna raised her poster anyway. "I was going to open with an Einstein quote about the eighth wonder of the world. Then I checked, and there's no reliable evidence he ever said it. So my new opening is: this graph is cool enough without a fake quote."

The class laughed, and Ms. Friedman smiled. "You just did what mathematicians do. You can infer nothing about a quote's truth from how famous the person is. You have to check the source."

At the end of class, Ellie peered at the two lines on the board, which curved apart with a kind of accidental symmetry, one straight and one bending. "So Einstein never said it, but the graph did all the talking anyway?"

"The graph," Arianna said, rolling up her poster, "never misquotes anybody."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
On Monday morning Emmett slid his new phone across the desk so Mouhamed could see it, and Mouhamed whistled low, the way he did when something good appeared in the room. "No way," Harriet said from the next row, leaning over to look. "It's the plan my dad picked," Emmett told her. "Texts and calls are free, and I get some data for the month." He had ridden the bus to school watching videos the whole way, and he planned to do the same thing going home.

By Friday the phone had stopped loading anything unless it was on Wi-Fi. At lunch Emmett sat staring at the little gray bar at the top of the screen. "It worked Monday," he said. "It worked Tuesday morning, too, I think. Then it just stopped." Harriet frowned. "You weren't texting that much, were you?" "Barely any," Emmett said. "A few messages to my dad." He turned the phone over in his hands. Something invisible had run out, and he wanted to know which thing it was.

In Ms. Ramírez's classroom, during the last ten minutes of silent reading, Emmett laid out the week like a math problem on scrap paper. He had watched videos on the bus every morning and every afternoon, except Thursday, when he forgot his earbuds and only texted. The messages were tiny; he'd written maybe twenty of them all week. The videos were the only other thing that used the phone away from home. So it had to be the videos. He thought of a way to test it, though the test felt almost too simple. He raised his hand. "Ms. Ramírez, is the classroom Wi-Fi the school's, not mine?" She nodded. "It's the school's, Emmett. Your plan isn't touched while you're on it."

After school Emmett adjusted his plan for the ride home. While he was still in the building, on the school's Wi-Fi, he downloaded three videos onto the phone. Then, on the bus, he turned off the mobile data and pressed play. The first video opened instantly, without bars, without loading. He watched Mouhamed's face as Mouhamed leaned across the aisle. "Wait, I thought your data died," Mouhamed said. "It did," Emmett said. "But streaming video eats it fast. Texting barely uses any at all. So now I download at school and watch after." It felt like the same bus and the same seat, but from a whole new perspective.

He tried one more thing before getting off. He sent his dad a message asking if they could look at the plan together this weekend, and the message went through on data, small and quick as anything. The phone buzzed back before his stop. "Yes. Also bring the charger." Emmett smiled, put the phone in his pocket, and stepped down into the afternoon.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
Matthew sat at the kitchen table while his dad read words from the official list. "Persimmon," his dad said, and Matthew spelled it, and his dad said "Correct," in the same flat voice the judges would use on Saturday. Last year Matthew had gone out in round three on "raspberry," because he had forgotten the silent p, and he had spent a whole year deciding that this time he would not just memorize but understand where spellings came from.

That was why he had gone to the library on Tuesday. While Abdul and Ali quizzed each other near the windows, Matthew had begun to excavate the reference shelf, pulling out heavy books one after another, and at the back he had found something strange: an enormous old dictionary, nearly as tall as his arm was long, with faded brown covers. He had opened it at random and found words spelled in ways he had never seen, some of them with alternatives, two spellings side by side for the same word. Who decided? he had wondered. Somebody must have, at some point, because the list his dad held had only one spelling for every word, and the judges would accept only that one.

He had carried the volume to the desk and asked the librarian about it. She had turned to the front of the book and shown him the page it came from. "Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755," she said. "It helped settle how many English words were spelled." Before that, she said, spellings wandered all over the place, which explained the doubled versions he had found. Matthew had copied the fact into his notebook, and he had read it again on the walk home, feeling the ground shift a little under his memorized lists. The words had not always been fixed. Someone had fixed them.

Now, on Friday night, the kitchen was tranquil except for the ticking clock and the scratch of his pencil. There was a knock, and Mr. Islam from next door stood at the door holding a plate of cookies, because he had heard about the regional bee. "You look like a candidate for some sugar," he said, setting the plate down. "Final round tomorrow?"

"Round six, if I make it," Matthew said. He pushed his notebook toward Mr. Islam, open to the fact he had copied. "Did you know this? That spellings weren't always settled?"

Mr. Islam read it and nodded slowly. "My grandmother used two spellings for the same word in her letters. Drove me crazy trying to read them."

Matthew's dad, drying a dish, glanced over. "So what does that change for you?"

"Nothing," Matthew started to say, and then stopped. He had planned to drill all night, word after word, until his eyes blurred. But if the spellings followed patterns someone had settled, then the patterns were the thing to learn, not just the lists. "Actually, everything," he said. "I'm going to group them. Silent letters together. Double letters together." He swept the flashcards into new piles, reshuffling his whole system with one night to go, his heart pounding at the risk of it.

At the table, Mr. Islam broke a cookie in half and handed a piece across.

"Try one," he said. "Champions eat first."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
The elevator in Great-Aunt Lin's building had buttons for one, two, three, and five. Noemie pressed five twice, thinking the first press had not taken, and watched the doors close on her cousins arguing about who would carry the fruit boxes up. Then Thalia nudged her. "It always does that," Thalia said. "There's no four in this whole building. My grandma says the word for four in Chinese sounds almost the same as the word for death, so they just skip it." She shrugged, like skipping a floor was the most ordinary thing in the world, and pressed five again as if to prove it.

Noemie's problem was in her backpack. She had brought Great-Aunt Lin a box of four tea cakes, wrapped in green paper, because her mother had said never arrive at a family gathering empty-handed, and four had seemed like a generous number. Now she counted them in her head and felt the package grow heavier on every floor the elevator did not bother to name. Five, six, seven. Her mother had also said you offer a gift with both hands and the receiver will refuse it once or twice before accepting, which Noemie had assumed was a joke until she saw it happen with the fruit.

At the door, Great-Aunt Lin took one look at the green wrapping and her eyebrows climbed. Noemie had read that green hats meant something unlucky too, so she began unwrapping the cakes herself, quickly, as if speed could fix anything. Then she slid three of them across the table and kept one in her pocket, saying she would eat it on the train home.

"Train home already?" said Great-Aunt Lin. "Sit. Eat first." She waved Noemie to the seat facing the door, the seat of honor, and pointed chopsticks at the lazy Susan. "Turn it toward your grandfather before you take anything. And no standing your chopsticks upright in the rice, that's for other occasions."

"I wasn't going to," Noemie said, though she had been about to.

Her grandfather, who was the conductor of a community orchestra and liked to cite old sayings at dinner, tapped his bowl with his chopsticks. "Three cakes," he observed in English, for her benefit. "Very good number. Three sounds like birth. Life."

"I know," said Noemie, who had known for exactly eleven minutes. She pulled the fourth cake out of her pocket anyway and set it on the lazy Susan, giving it a slow spin.

"Four," said Great-Aunt Lin. "Take that one home, sweetheart."

Noemie ate it on the train, feeling considerably less impoverished of cake than she had planned.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
story:
The problem started when Mael refused to believe him. "Summer is hot because Earth is closer to the sun," Mael said, digging his toes into the hot sand. "Everybody knows that." George opposed this idea instantly, mostly because he'd read the opposite in Ms. Sato's science book, but he couldn't actually prove it. Earth's tilt causing seasons was not something you could see from a beach towel.

"We need a flashlight," Albert said. He ran to the lifeguard's station, where Ms. Sato, their neighbour, was reading under an umbrella. She lent him a small transparent plastic one, the kind with a blue casing, and told them not to drop it in the ocean.

George switched it on and held it straight over the sand. "Look. Small circle, and it's bright." He traced the ring of light with his finger. Then he tilted the flashlight at an angle, the way Earth's axis leans, and the light stretched out into a long, pale oval. "Same light," he said slowly, feeling his own mind change as he watched. "But now it's spread over more sand. So each bit of sand gets less." He tilted it further and the glow got wider and dimmer still.

"So in summer," Albert said, crouching down, "the sunlight comes down more straight, like this, and the same light is packed onto a smaller spot, so it heats it more?" George nodded. He stuck one hand in the small bright circle and one in the wide dim oval. The bright patch felt warmer within seconds, though he wasn't sure if that was real or just his imagination. Mael still looked stubborn, so George grabbed a stick and wrote in the wet sand where the waves had just retreated: "Tilt, not distance. Direct light = small + hot. Tilted light = wide + dim + cooler." The foam hissed in and erased it, which Mael said was the ocean disagreeing, but he was grinning when he said it.

That evening George wrote a message on a postcard and left it under a shell on Ms. Sato's porch, since she had asked to know how their experiment turned out. "Dear Ms. Sato," he wrote. "We proved the tilt thing. When the flashlight pointed straight down the circle was small and bright, and when we tilted it the light got wide and dim. So summer is when your part of Earth gets the direct light. Also, the hermit crab in the tide pool had camouflage exactly the colour of the sand, and Mael stepped on a jellyfish but it was fine." He drew a little Earth with a leaning axis at the bottom.

The next morning Ms. Sato caught up with him on the boardwalk, postcard in hand. "One correction," she said. "That was a piece of seaweed Mael stepped on." She held out a thermos. "Hot chocolate for the young scientist?" George took the cup and pointed at the sun climbing over the water. "Direct light," he said. "Small, bright, hot." Mael, from down the beach, cupped his hands and yelled, "Tilt! I believe you now!"

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Ellie sat on her bedroom floor with a photocopy of a settler's diary spread in front of her and her laptop open beside it. Ms. Brennan had assigned each student one primary source and one question to answer with it, and Ellie's question was why the Bennett family had left Ohio for the Oregon Trail in 1846. The trouble was that the diary, kept by fourteen-year-old Ada Bennett, never once said why. Ada wrote about oxen, about her little brother's fever, about how her mother cried the first night on the trail. She wrote about everything except leaving.

Ellie's first instinct was to guess that they wanted adventure, because that was the reason in every movie she had ever seen. But when she tried to write it down, the words felt wrong. "They left because it seemed exciting" did not fit a mother crying. She texted Paul, whose source was a letter from a gold miner, and he wrote back that his guy had a reason on every page. Lucky him. Ellie read Ada's first entry again, hunting for anything she had missed, and stopped at a sentence near the bottom: "Father says we can begin again where the land is cheap and no one remembers what we lost."

What had they lost? Ellie read every entry with that question in her head, like a flashlight she was shining backward through the pages. In the third entry Ada mentioned they had sold the spinning wheel, and in the fifth, that Father had taken work hauling stone for other men, which Ada called strange for a farmer with his own fields. Farmers did not haul stone for other men unless something had gone wrong with the fields. It was like finding footprints and trying to picture the animal, Ellie thought. She could not see the cause, only the marks it left.

She searched the diary's introduction, written by a librarian, and there it was in a footnote: the Panic of 1837. Her mom, carrying laundry past the door, asked what a panic was, and Ellie said, "It was a money collapse in 1837 that turned into a long economic depression," reading it almost straight off the page. Then she checked the dates. The diary said the Bennetts lost their farm in 1841, four years after the panic began, right in the middle of the depression. Ruined farmers were heading west looking for cheap, fertile land, and the Bennetts were one of those families. Ellie could finally see the whole shape of it.

Paul called that evening, sounding indifferent to her excitement, mostly wanting to complain about his miner's terrible spelling. "Then swap with me," Ellie said. But when she opened her essay to write her conclusion, she found a twist she had not expected. In the last entry, Ada wrote that Father had a brother in Oregon who had begged them to come for years, even before the farm was lost. So there were two reasons stacked on top of each other, one pulling and one pushing, and the panic alone would not have told the whole story. Ellie highlighted the sentence and asked her mom, "Can a person have two reasons for one decision?"

Her mom set the laundry basket down. "Ask Ada," she said, nodding at the diary. Ellie turned back to the photocopy, pencil in hand, and underlined: "We go because we must, and because Uncle Joseph says the plums there grow as big as your fist."

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Watercolour is transparent, so each wash lets the layers beneath show through; that is why painters work from light to dark, because a dark wash cannot be covered by a lighter one.
story:
Declan set his sketchbook on the picnic table in Mehtab's backyard and stared at the pencil outline of his grandfather's face, wishing for the tenth time that he had inherited his mother's talent for art instead of her terrible handwriting. Watercolour kit open. Three brushes. A jar of water so clean it looked like glass. Mr. Hoang, the neighbour whose fence they were technically leaning against, had offered one piece of advice over the fence last week: "Watercolour is transparent, so you work light to dark. Each wash lets the layers beneath show through, because a dark wash can't be covered by a lighter one." Declan had nodded, but he hadn't really believed it. How could paint be like stained glass? Paint covered things. Paint was the covering-est stuff in the world.

So he started with the part that seemed most important: the hair. His grandfather had magnificent silver-black hair, and Declan wanted it bold. He mixed a strong dark wash and painted it in first, feeling very efficient, very systematic, like an engineer. Paige, sprawled on the grass beside Mehtab, watched him lay a pale grey over the hair to soften it. The pale grey vanished. It just disappeared into the dark, like a whisper into a thunderstorm. Declan tried white. Nothing. He tried pale grey again, harder, as if pressing harder had ever fixed anything in the history of watercolour. The highlight he had planned for the top of the hair, that shine that made Grandpa look like Grandpa, would not appear.

"Did the paper eat it?" Mehtab asked, leaning over. "Or did the dark eat it?"

"Nothing ate it," Declan muttered, but he was already wondering. He painted a dark stripe on scrap paper, let it dry, then painted a light stripe over half of it. The light stripe showed up on the white paper and simply was not there on the dark half. Then he flipped the order on a fresh scrap: light stripe first, dark over top. The dark sat on it fine. He did it twice more, because a scientist never trusts one trial. Same result every time. He sat back slowly. It wasn't that his paint was broken. It was that the paint never covered anything. Every layer was a sheet of coloured glass, and glass couldn't hide glass.

"Paint it backward," Paige said. "Face first, skin tones, all the pale stuff, then hair last."

"Like stacking shadows," Declan said. "Lightest shadow first."

He started over. Pale peach washes for the skin, built up in thin patient layers until a nose appeared out of nowhere, which felt honestly like a magic trick. Cheeks, then darker creases, then finally, last of all, the hair, laid down dark over everything and glowing like it had depth because the layers beneath it still showed through. It looked, if he squinted and held it at arm's length, roughly like a human being. Mehtab said it looked like a wizard. Declan decided that was a compliment.

Mr. Hoang appeared at the fence with his watering can and studied the painting. "You learned it the good way," he said.

"The hard way," Declan said.

"Those are the same way," said Mr. Hoang, and watered his tomatoes.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
story:
The ad appeared between two videos on Matteo's phone: a man in a suit standing in front of a rocket, saying the new productivity app would "change your life forever." Matteo squinted at it. Behind him, Phillip and Shayan were arguing about whether the cafeteria's mystery meat was actually turkey, which was at least an argument you could settle by asking somebody.

"It changed my life," Matteo said, holding up the phone. "That's what the guy says."

"So it works," Phillip said.

"How would I know if it works?" Matteo said. "He doesn't say what it does. He doesn't say by when. He just says it changes lives."

Shayan leaned over the seat. "Then try it and find out."

"That's the problem," Matteo said. "Even if I tried it, what would I look for? If my life didn't change, they'd just say I wasn't using it right, or it takes a year, or it changes your inner life, whatever that means." He scrolled down, looking for the fine print. "There's nothing here that could ever be proven wrong. That's the trick. It's not even really a claim. It's a claim that can't be checked even in principle, so it gives you nothing to test."

Phillip frowned. "The turkey question we could test, though. We could ask Ms. Kaur. She monitors the lunch line."

"She would know," Shayan agreed. "Or we could follow the delivery truck."

"And the app," Matteo said, "nobody could ever check it. Not you, not the emperor of the whole world, not a scientist with a lab. If you can't check something, you can't argue about it. You can only shrug." He bookmarked the ad anyway, because Ms. Kaur had said their persuasive writing unit started Monday, and he suspected this was exactly the kind of thing she wanted them to notice.

The bus lurched around the corner by the old arcade, the one with the asteroid game where a little ship tried to orbit a dying sun. Phillip pointed at it. "That place is so obsolete it hurts."

"Everything in there changes lives," Matteo said. "Forever. No refunds."

Shayan laughed so hard he knocked his water bottle into the aisle, and it rolled all the way up to the driver's feet and stopped there, spinning slowly, like a tiny planet nobody could argue with.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Jake spread his sketchbook on the picnic table and stabbed his pencil at the blank page. "Today I learn one-point perspective. For real this time."

Florent dropped onto the bench across from him, holding his own pad. "Mr. Pierre says the assignment is mandatory, even for people like me who draw stick figures."

"Then you're lucky you're with me." Jake drew a horizontal line across the middle of his page and marked a dot on it. "See, this is the horizon line, and this dot is the vanishing point. Every edge of the street goes toward it. The sidewalk lines, the rooftops, all of them." He sketched fast, sweeping lines from the edges of the paper straight to the dot, then boxed them in with vertical lines for buildings. A street appeared, flat on the page but somehow deep, like you could walk down it.

Mariah came through the gate with her sketchbook under her arm. "I already started mine. I sat on my front curb this morning and drew our street." She flipped her pad open. Her street looked strange to Jake at first. The road filled most of the page, tall and looming, and the sky was only a thin strip at the top.

"That looks like a giant drew it," Florent said.

"It looks like I'm little," Mariah said. "Because I was. I was sitting on the curb." She tapped her page. "My horizon line ended up way down here, near the bottom."

Jake stared at his own drawing. His horizon line sat in the middle, and the street felt like it belonged to nobody, floating at no height at all. He grabbed a fresh sheet and drew the horizon line high, almost at the top edge, then ran all his lines to the vanishing point again. The street dropped away below, tiny and distant, the way a street looks from upstairs.

"That's like my bedroom window," Mariah said, leaning over his shoulder. "Draw our street from up there, Jake. Then we'll have the same street twice."

"Same street, three views." Jake was already penciling in windows on the far-off buildings, small as rice grains. He held up Mariah's page beside his. "You can't even measure the difference with a ruler, but I bet you could quantify it. Percentage of page that's road versus sky."

Florent snorted. "You two are writing a math problem about a drawing."

"It's better than a poem," Jake said. "A stanza repeats a line with one thing changed. We're repeating a whole street."

Florent pulled his pad closer and drew his horizon line halfway up, then stopped. "Wait. If it's low, I'm a kid on the curb. If it's high, I'm up at a window. Where's mine?"

"Anywhere," Mariah said. "That's the fun part. Where do you want to be standing?"

Florent pressed his pencil down and slid the horizon line to the very bottom of the page. "Curb," he said. "Definitely the curb."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
story:
Caleb's German teacher had assigned one page, due Friday: describe your family and your pets in full sentences. Caleb had a mother, a father, a little sister, one dog named Biscuit, and a goldfish that was technically his sister's but ate Caleb's fish food, so he counted it. He typed his first sentence into the class tablets: "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze." He did not have a cat, but Biscuit deserved a companion on paper.

The tablet underlined "hund" and "katze" in wavy red lines, which Caleb took personally. He checked the spelling twice, letter by letter. H-u-n-d. K-a-t-z-e. The spell-checker disagreed anyway, waving its little red flags like a crossing guard who hated him.

Across the room, Hunter was typing fast, capitals scattered through his sentences like birdseed. Caleb leaned over. Hunter had written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," and no red lines anywhere. Not one.

"Your shift key is broken," Caleb whispered.

"It's not," Hunter whispered back.

Caleb looked at his screen, then at Hunter's, then at his own again. He tested something small. He changed "hund" to "Hund" only, leaving "katze" lowercase. The wavy line under Hund vanished. The one under katze stayed. He capitalized "katze." Gone too. So the checker wasn't hunting misspellings, because the letters had been right all along. It was hunting lowercase words that Hunter had uppercase. He scanned more of Hunter's sentences. "Mutter," "Vater," "Schwester," every single one began with a capital. Even "Fisch."

"In German, every noun begins with a capital letter," Hunter said, shrugging. "That's all it is."

Caleb sat with that for a second, feeling the shape of the rule. Not the pets, not the sister, just any noun, big or small. He typed a new sentence about his goldfish and hit capitalize with a kind of ceremony. "Ich habe einen Fisch." Clean. Luminous, even, in its red-line-free way. He began to suspect the humiliation of the past ten minutes had been entirely avoidable.

Then Ms. Choi stopped behind his screen. "Nice work, Caleb. One thing. You wrote that your dog is a cat."

He looked at the sentence. "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze." He had copied Hunter's capitals and, somewhere in the shuffle, Hunter's pets too. Hunter, it turned out, had two cats and no dog, and was watching Caleb now with the calm interest of someone whose homework had just become twice as good.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
