The line at Kelly's Gas and Go stretched past the air pump before Parker even got his bike parked. Every pump was taken, and a man in a delivery van sat with his engine running, tapping his horn. Serena waved from beside the ice machine, where she and Kole were watching the crowd. "Radio says the ice storm hits at seven," she said. "My mom sent me to fill the spare can for the generator. Yours too?"

Parker held up the five-gallon can. His family's furnace had died that morning, and the repairman couldn't come until next week because he was booked solid with other broken furnaces. The generator in the garage would run the space heaters tonight, but only if there was gas in it by seven o'clock. That gave him just over two hours. He counted the cars. Nine, ten, eleven, and more pulling in off the road every minute.

Mr. Kelly came out with a pole and changed the price sign himself, which he never did. Parker squinted at the new number. Yesterday the regular price had been three dollars and ten cents. The sign now read three eighty-nine. A woman at pump two leaned out her window and shouted at Mr. Kelly, and he shouted back something Parker couldn't hear, and the line barely moved. Kole checked his phone. "Every station in town is jammed. The app says prices are all over the place, going up and down all day." The prices didn't just sit still, Parker thought; they fluctuated, like the numbers on his dad's weather app.

"Watch the pumps," Parker said suddenly. "Not the cars. The pumps." Serena frowned, but Kole got it. At two ninety-nine, the station further down the road, there had been a line a block long, and people were topping off half-full tanks and filling spare cans besides. Here, at three eighty-nine, drivers pumped less. A man shut off his nozzle at fifteen dollars and left with a tank only half full. A teenage driver looked at the sign, swore, and drove off without buying anything. Fewer dollars, fewer gallons, fewer buyers. When the price rose, people bought less. Parker remembered the lemonade stand last summer, when Serena's sister had doubled her price from fifty cents to a dollar and the sidewalk in front of her table had gone empty by noon. When the price fell back, the line came back too.

"It's called the law of demand," Serena said, snapping her fingers. "Mr. Kelly had it on a poster in the back. People buy more when the price drops and less when it climbs, as long as nothing else changes." Parker shifted the gas can to his other hand and checked the sky, which had gone the color of a nickel. The line crawled. Sixty-one minutes to seven. He watched the pump nearest the road, where the man in the van was now arguing with Mr. Kelly about the new price. Mr. Kelly crossed his arms and pointed at the empty half of his lot, the half where the tanks were low, the half that would stay empty until tomorrow's truck came, if the truck could get through the ice at all. "You want it or not?" Mr. Kelly called. "Last can goes to the kid with the generator." Parker stepped forward.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
story:
The wind on the back straight of the track had a habit of shoving Maya sideways, and today it was worse than ever. Mr. Buchanan had written her name on the list for the eight-hundred-metre race at Friday's meet, and she had exactly three practices to figure out the one thing that kept ruining her: the first lap always felt easy, and the second lap always felt like her legs belonged to someone else. Piper handed her a folded note as they walked out of science class. "You looked miserable at practice," it read, "so I timed you. Lap one, forty-three seconds. Lap two, sixty-one. Something is eating you alive on that second lap. Also, you still owe me a granola bar from the commerce we did at lunch on Tuesday. Two granola bars, actually, since you never paid up. Piper." Maya laughed, then frowned at the numbers. Sixty-one seconds. Where did eighteen whole seconds go?

She decided to run the practice laps like a scientist instead of a racer. On Monday she went out hard, exactly the way her rebellious legs always wanted to, and paid for it on lap two, dying so badly that Zachariah, jogging beside the fence, called out, "You look like a melted popsicle." On Tuesday she tried going out slow, and although she finished stronger, her total time was still terrible. Neither plan explained the missing seconds. The problem, she realized, wasn't only how fast she ran. It was something invisible that changed from lap to lap.

The wind. On the back straight, where the track curved away from the gym, the gusts hit her full in the face both laps, and she could feel the extra work in her shoulders. But Piper, running just ahead of her on Tuesday, had seemed to float through that stretch. Maya chewed on the puzzle during math class, doodling little arrows in her notebook. The wind blew at everyone. Piper wasn't stronger than her. What was different about where they ran?

On Wednesday she tested it. She tucked in directly behind Zachariah on the back straight, close enough to see the tag on his shirt, and held that spot the whole first lap while he battled the gusts. It felt strangely calm back there, quiet and steady, like running indoors. When she swung out for the second lap, her legs still had bounce in them, and she finished her fastest practice time all week. "You were right on my shoulder," Zachariah said afterward, gulping water. "You were drafting me." "Drafting," Maya repeated, holding the word like a prize. So that was it. Running directly behind another runner sheltered her from the wind, and that meant following someone on the first lap could save her energy for the finish.

At the meet on Friday the wind was howling across the back straight, and Piper was in her heat, seeded one lane and one spot ahead. Maya stayed calm when the gun cracked, letting the field string out, then slid in behind Piper's shoulder at the first turn. Down the back straight the gusts bent the flags sideways, and Maya tucked closer, feeling the calm pocket open up in front of her while the wind worked on Piper instead. Around the final bend, with two hundred metres left, she still had something in her legs. She swung wide, kicked, and heard Piper yell over the wind, "Sneaky, Maya! I'm collecting a granola bar tax for that!" Maya crossed the line, looked up at the clock, and grinned so wide the wind nearly dried her teeth.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never contained the metal lead; the name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Aubrey had signed up for the Saturday printmaking class at the community art studio because she wanted to make a poster for her cousin Dev's birthday, and she was the only twelve-year-old there who hadn't touched a printing press before. Mr. Sultani, who ran the studio, set out pencils, carving blocks, and ink, and told everyone to sketch a design first.

She was halfway through drawing a dragon when she found the note folded at the bottom of her supply bag. It was from Dev, who was seven. "I am not coming to your art thing," it said. "Mom says the studio prohibits eating near the ink, which is fine, but I licked a pencil yesterday at school and I think I have lead poisoning. Please cancel my birthday. Sorry. Dev."

Aubrey read it twice. Then she looked at the pencil in her own hand. She had chewed on pencils her whole life, and so had Krystal, who sat beside her carving a moon into a block, and neither of them had ever gotten sick. If pencils really carried lead, half the kids in her grade would be poisoned by now. That did not add up.

She raised her hand anyway. "Mr. Sultani, do pencils have lead in them?"

"Look in the supply drawer," he said, pointing. "Third one down."

In the drawer she found the box the pencils had come in, and on the side of it, in small print, the word graphite. She turned the box over, and there was more: a short paragraph about how the stuff inside a pencil had never contained the metal lead at all. Early writers had mistaken graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the wrong name had stuck. Aubrey stood there holding the box, thinking about the irony of it. Everyone went around calling it lead, and nobody had ever put lead in it.

"So what's inside?" Krystal asked, leaning over.

"Graphite," Aubrey said. "Not lead. The name came from early writers who mistook graphite for a kind of lead ore."

"Then why does everyone call it lead?"

"Because the mistake never woke up," Aubrey said. "It's been dormant for hundreds of years." She put the box back and pulled out her phone.

She wrote a message to Dev's tablet, since he answered messages faster than letters: "You don't have lead poisoning. Pencils never had lead in them. The gray stuff is graphite. People used the wrong word ages ago and never fixed it. Also I'm still making your poster, and you're still having a birthday." She pressed send.

Then she went back to her dragon, pressed the finished print that afternoon, and mailed it in a cardboard tube with the pencil taped to the outside. On the label she wrote, in careful letters, "Safe to lick. Still don't."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
At dinner on Tuesday, Alexander pushed his noodles around his plate and finally said, "Something's wrong with Skyler, and I can't figure out what." She had stopped sitting with them at lunch, and last week she quit the track team right before the big meet. Nothing had happened that he could see. No fight, no falling grade, nothing. It was like watching steam vanish off the pavement and trying to guess where it went. He kept coming back to the question: what was the hidden cause?

"She told me something in September," his mother said, setting down the water pitcher. "She'd been worrying so much for so long that she couldn't sleep, and it was getting in the way of school. So her mom took her to a doctor."

"Like she was sick?" Alexander asked.

"Not exactly like a cold," his mother said. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, though. Everybody does."

Alexander frowned. He got nervous before spelling bees, but it passed by the next morning. Skyler's worry hadn't passed. It had lasted a long time, and it was intense enough to knock her off the track team, which was weird because Skyler was the most robust runner in their grade. His father said worry was a common phenomenon, like weather, and Alexander thought that was a strange comparison until he realized weather was invisible too. You only saw what it did to things.

"Mom. If it's normal, why did she need a doctor?"

His mother tilted her head, the way she did when she wanted him to work it out himself. "What did I say about how long it lasted and what it was doing to her life?"

Alexander repeated it slowly, like laying out puzzle pieces. Normal worry comes and goes. Skyler's had stayed, gotten huge, and blocked everything. So maybe there was a point where normal turned into something else, the way a whole fog condenses out of clear air. "There's probably a name for that," he said.

"There is," his mother said. "Skyler told me her doctor diagnosed her with an anxiety disorder."

"Is that bad?"

His mother shook her head. "She said it's treatable. She's been learning ways of coping with it, and she's setting boundaries, like taking a break from the team for a while until things feel steadier."

The next day at school, Alexander slid his tray across from Skyler at lunch, even though she was sitting alone at the far table. "You don't have to talk about it," he said. "But you don't have to eat alone, either."

Skyler looked up, and then at the empty seat, and then back at him. "You're the first one who just sat down," she said. "Everyone else keeps asking if I'm okay."

"I'm working on a theory about that," Alexander said, and handed her a roll.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
story:
The campfire had burned down to orange coals when Micheal said the word "tilt," and Paige's whole plan for the evening fell apart. She was supposed to present her science project tomorrow, a talk on why Earth has seasons, and she had counted on one more night of practice. Instead Mr. Nair, who led the camping trip, had gathered everyone around the fire for marshmallows, and now half the class was arguing about whether winter happened because Earth moved farther from the sun.

"That's not it," Paige said, waving her roasting stick. "Earth stays basically the same distance away. It's the tilt of the axis."

Asma laughed so hard she nearly dropped her marshmallow into the ashes. "Tilt? Four seasons? Paige, where my grandmother lives, we would laugh at that. It is hot all year. Near the equator the sunlight stays direct the whole year, so the temperature barely changes. We don't have warm and cold seasons at all. We have wet seasons and dry seasons. That's it."

"Wet and dry?" Micheal said. "That's only two. That's not even half of four."

"Two is plenty," Asma said, "when one of them is rain like a waterfall."

Paige chewed the burnt edge of her marshmallow and thought. Two seasons. No cold. Sunlight direct all year. In her head she held the globe from Mr. Nair's truck, the one with the line drawn around its middle, and she turned it slowly. If the axis tilted, the middle of the globe never leaned away from the light. Only the top and bottom took turns leaning toward it and away.

"I need a flashlight," she said, standing up so fast she almost knocked over the thermos. "And something round."

"Here," Asma said, and held out an orange from the snack bag without being asked, because she had noticed Paige's hands were sticky and gave her a napkin too. Micheal trotted to the tent and came back with his headlamp, its obstinate strap refusing to stay tight until he bit it and yanked the buckle with his teeth.

Paige drew a line around the orange's middle with her finger. "Equator." She shone the headlamp straight down and tilted the orange. "Look. The top leans toward the light, so it's spread out and strong up there. Now watch the middle." The stripe she had drawn stayed bright and direct no matter how far she tipped it. "So near the equator, the light stays direct all year. It never gets weak, never gets strong. Nothing to change the temperature much. So no warm season, no cold season."

"So the rain does the changing instead," Asma said slowly, leaning in. "Wet, then dry, then wet. Like breathing."

"That is so weird," Micheal said. "My brain feels like it's being turned inside out, like an intestine or something."

"Do not compare my orange to an intestine," Paige said. "I'm going to eat this orange."

They were quiet for a moment, the coals popping, moths bumping the headlamp. Paige had been ready to abandon her project and ask Mr. Nair for a new topic an hour ago, and now she had the best part of her whole talk sitting in her palm, tilting in the firelight.

"Can I hold the orange while you do this tomorrow?" Asma asked. "I'll be the equator's lawyer."

"Only if you say wet and dry seasons in that exact voice you just used."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale; otherwise a short bar may stand for more rain.
story:
Quinn spread two climate graphs across the kitchen table, one for a desert city and one for a rainforest city, and weighted the corners with mugs from the drying rack. Her project was due Monday, and her plan was simple: look at the bars, decide which place was wetter, write a paragraph. Tim and Rosemary were coming over at three, but she wanted her answer ready before they arrived so she could argue with confidence.

They showed up early, arguing already. "Phoenix is way drier," Tim said, dropping his backpack on a chair. "Look at that rainforest graph. The bars are gigantic."

"No, look at the desert one," Rosemary said, tapping the page. "See how tall the August bar is? That's real rain. That city gets plenty."

Quinn leaned over both graphs, comparing the height of the bars. The rainforest bars were about four times taller, so Tim seemed right. But something bothered her, the way a wobbly shelf bothers you even before anything falls off it. She checked the months, then the temperature lines, then the small print along the side of each graph.

"Wait," she said. She pointed at the numbers stacked beside the rainfall bars. "This one counts by tens. Twenty, forty, sixty. The other one counts by fifties. Two hundred, four hundred." The tall rainforest bar for March topped out at two hundred millimetres. The short desert bar for August stood for sixty. "You can't just look at bar height," she said slowly. "The rainfall axes have to use the same scale, or the bars aren't speaking the same language."

"Then which city is actually wetter?" Rosemary asked.

"The rainforest one, still, but not by as much as it looked. And Rosemary, that August bar in the desert isn't some weird anomaly. It's just a normal summer storm, on a different scale." She grabbed a ruler and drew a fresh set of axes, using the same numbers for both cities, then re-drew the bars so they could be compared fairly. Tim watched over her shoulder and admitted, quietly, that he had nearly written "ten times rainier" in his report.

When Quinn's mother came home, the three of them were taping the new graph to the poster board, and Ms. Almeida from next door was at the door holding a plate of brownies. "Heard there was a science project," she said. Quinn held up the poster. "We verified it ourselves," she said. "Same scale, then compare."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A climate graph usually shows each month's average temperature as a line and each month's average rainfall as bars on the same chart.
story:
Kaylee spread three books across the library table like she was planning a tiny rebellion against homework itself. "Ms. Mori says we have to compare a desert and a rainforest," she told Andi and Leila, who had come along mostly for the air conditioning. "And she says to use climate graphs. Easy." She flipped to the page on the Sonoran Desert and squinted. "Okay, so the temperature in the desert is super high all year. Look at these bars. Some of them are enormous."

Leila leaned over. "That seems weird. The bars go way up in summer, but they also go way up in the rainforest graph, and the rainforest graph you showed me has tall bars too. The desert can't be as wet as the rainforest."

"It can't," Kaylee said slowly. "That's the whole point of the assignment." She pulled the second book closer, then the third, comparing pages. Both deserts had short bars. Both rainforests had tall ones. "Wait." She traced her finger along a thin line zigzagging across the top of each chart. "There's a line too. I thought it was decoration."

Andi snorted. "Charts don't come with decoration. That would be vigorous decorating." She tapped the line. "Maybe that's the temperature, and the bars are the rain."

Kaylee tested it. In the desert graph, the line stayed high while the bars stayed stubby, which matched what she knew: hot and dry. In the rainforest graph, the line stayed warm and the bars towered, which matched wet. If the bars were temperature, the rainforest would somehow be boiling and the desert would be drowning, and neither made sense. "So the line is temperature," she said, "and the bars are each month's rainfall. They're on the same chart the whole time."

"How do we quantify the difference for the write-up?" Leila asked, hunting for the math. "Do we count bar heights?"

"Ms. Mori said compare, so we compare." Kaylee grabbed a pencil and started a two-column list: line high, bars short for the desert; line steady, bars huge for the rainforest. Andi added a drawing of a very sweaty cactus next to a very smug fern, and Leila labeled them "Team Dry" and "Team Damp."

At the front desk, Ms. Mori glanced at Kaylee's notebook. "So what did the graphs tell you?"

"That I spent ten minutes thinking rain was heat," Kaylee said. "Also that deserts and rainforests are basically opposites."

"Then it was a good ten minutes," said Ms. Mori, and stamped the books with a cheerful thunk. Andi held up the cactus drawing. "He forgives you," she said.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats.
story:
Tristan carried the cardboard box across Ridgeway Park with both hands, because the woman at the shelter had said a puppy could wriggle out of anything. Inside, a black-and-white puppy nosed at the air holes. His parents had made him wait two years for this, and only after he agreed to enroll in the shelter's free puppy-care class the following Saturday. The smell of cut grass and someone's charcoal grill drifted over the path.

Everlee waved from the picnic tables near the fountain, where she was spreading out her lunch. She had texted him three times that morning asking what kind of dog he was getting, because she wanted to be the first to meet it. "Let me see, let me see," she said, and Tristan set the box down on the bench beside her trail mix, which was open in a plastic bag.

The puppy tumbled out, stepped on Everlee's knee, and licked her wrist. She laughed and held up a handful of trail mix. "Want some, buddy? There's raisins in here, he loves fruit probably."

"No, wait." Tristan remembered the shelter woman pointing at a poster on the wall, the one with a bowl of grapes crossed out in red. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats." He had thought it was odd, since raisins were just dried grapes, but he had repeated it to himself on the bus anyway.

Everlee froze with her hand in the air. "Seriously?"

"Seriously."

She lowered the trail mix and closed the bag, and Tristan noticed something. There were small purple smears on the puppy's whiskers. His stomach dropped. While he had been reading the adoption papers at the other bench, the puppy had been out of the box, and Everlee's bag had been tipped on its side. A cluster of raisins lay scattered under the table, and three were missing from the pile.

"How many did he eat?" Tristan asked.

"I don't know, I wasn't watching. Two? Three?" Everlee's voice went thin. The park suddenly felt too big and too slow. Tristan picked up the puppy, felt its heartbeat against his palm, fast as a hummingbird, and made a decision. "We have to call the vet. The shelter gave me a number."

Ms. Georgiou, who taught science at his school and was reading on the next bench, looked up. "Is something wrong with that puppy?" Tristan explained, holding out the scattered raisins as evidence. She drove them to the animal clinic in her green hatchback, the puppy whining softly on Everlee's lap the whole way, while Tristan called the vet's office from Everlee's phone and was told to come at once.

The vet gave the puppy something to make it throw up, and it did, right into a metal pan. Then she said he would be fine, because they had come quickly. Tristan sat in the waiting room with the bill in his hand, his first act of commerce as a pet owner, paid partly with his birthday money. He texted his parents, then looked at Everlee.

"From now on, no food on the bench," he said.

"Permanent rule," said Everlee. "I'll check everything. Even my granola bars."

The puppy, sleepy and wobbly, licked Tristan's thumb once and fell asleep in his jacket.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Anais slid the slide onto the microscope stage and clamped it down with the brass clips. The onion skin that Mr. Pham had cut from the inner curve of the bulb was thinner than tissue paper, and she had stained it herself, one careful drop of iodine. At forty times magnification she saw rows of bricks, pale gold and neatly parallel, like a wall built by someone very patient. She turned the knob and the cells snapped into focus, sharp at the edges.

The worksheet had three arrows to label. Cell wall, easy. Nucleus, easy, a dark blot near the middle of each brick. Cell membrane, the third arrow pointed at the outer edge of a cell, and Anais could not find anything there to point at. She looked at the edge where one cell met the next. There was a line, but it looked like a single line, not two. She labeled the wall on that line and left the membrane blank.

Sebastien leaned over from the next stool. "You done?"

"I can't find the membrane." She pulled back so he could see. "Maybe onion cells just don't have one."

"They have one. We're all made of cells, and every cell has a membrane. It's in the book, page sixty."

"Then where is it?" Anais said. She looked again. Sebastien's slide was a different piece of skin, stained darker, and his cells looked the same at the edges. One line. Precious, across the table, had drawn her membrane arrow touching the same line as her wall arrow, which struck Anais as cheating.

She sat with it for a minute. The line at the edge could be two lines lying on top of each other, so close they looked like one. She thought of the track behind the school, where one runner passing another on the inside lane could look, from the bleachers, like a single runner until the moment they separated. If the membrane was pressed right against the wall, it would be invisible as its own line. It would only look missing.

She tested it the only way she could, with the fine focus. She turned the knob a hair at a time, watching the edge of a cell while the focus moved through the thickness of the skin. For one fraction of a turn, the single line seemed to double, just barely, and then it closed again like a mouth. She did it twice more to be sure.

She wrote her labels. Wall and membrane, both on the outside edge, one pressed against the inside of the other. "It's there," she said. "You just can't see it as a separate line, because it's pressed so tightly against the wall." Then she nudged Precious's elbow. "Fix your arrow. Yours is fine, but you're going to want to draw it where mine is."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
story:
Madison leaned closer to the screen, where her message from Bennett glowed in the chat window. "My grandpa says Maple Ridge was founded by a guy named Cornelius Vale who gave everyone free land," he had typed. "Ms. Farah-Ali says we need a source for our town history project. Tell me if you find one."

The problem was that half the internet said one thing and half said another. One site claimed Vale arrived in 1841 with a wagon train. Another said the town began in 1848 when a railroad camp turned permanent. A third was so vague it only mentioned "brave pioneers" and "a generous founder," with no names, no dates, nothing she could grab onto. Madison scrolled and scrolled. Which of these, she wondered, was just somebody's opinion, and which was something she could actually check?

Then she remembered what Ms. Farah-Ali had said on Friday, almost in passing: "A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim." Madison said the words out loud to herself. A letter. A photograph. Official data. Not somebody's website about somebody's website.

The town library's digitized newspaper archive was linked right there on the library page, and it went back to the 1840s. She typed "Vale" into the search box and held her breath. An article from 1847 appeared, written by a reporter who had apparently interviewed Cornelius Vale himself at the land office. Vale had offered parcels at two dollars an acre, the article said, not free. There was even a photograph of the land office ledger, with names and payments inked down the page in careful rows.

So the "free land" story was a claim, and now she had checked it against a primary source. But wait, she thought. What if the newspaper had gotten it wrong too? She searched further and found the land office's official data from the same year, digitized by the county. The numbers matched the ledger photograph. Two different firsthand records from the time, agreeing with each other. That felt like something solid.

She pasted the links into her reply to Bennett. "Primary source says two dollars an acre. Grandpa's story is an opinion," she typed. "Ask him where he heard it. Maybe his grandpa told him." Then she sat back and looked at the photograph of the ledger again, at all those names in faded ink. Somewhere in that list, she realized, might be her own last name. She leaned in and began to read down the columns, one line at a time.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
story:
Justin spread his brushes across the library table and stared at the poster he was supposed to finish by Saturday. It advertised the community theater audition on Sunday, and Mr. Doyle planned to hang it right over the returns desk where everyone would see it. The letters were done. The problem was the sunset behind them, which had turned the color of wet dirt for the third afternoon in a row.

"You mixed them again," said Tyrell, sliding into the chair across from him. Tyrell had come to work on his own poster for the summer reading contest, but mostly he was watching Justin suffer.

"I followed the same steps." Justin held up the failed attempt. "I put in the red for the low sky, then I blended up toward the green I mixed for the top, because the poster colors for the audition notice are red and green." Every time the two colors met in the middle, a dull brown smeared across the paper instead of a smooth sunset. He had started to dread picking up the brush at all.

He got up and pulled a book on painting from the shelf, the one with a big circle of colors inside. Red sat on one side. Green sat exactly across from it. He ran his finger around the circle to be sure. "They're opposite each other," he said slowly. "On the color wheel." Tyrell leaned over to look.

"So?"

"So every time I blend them in the middle, I get mud. Watch." Justin took a scrap of paper and touched red to it, then green beside it, then dragged a wet brush through both. The scrap went gray-brown, the exact color ruining his sunset. He tried orange and blue next, and green and red again just to be certain, and each pair darkened the same dull way. "The opposites do it. Every pair I try." He glanced at the book's chart. "Complementary," he read off the page. "That's what they're called when they sit across from each other."

Justin sat back down, flipped to fresh paper, and drew a quick pencil line dividing the sky in two. Instead of blending the red upward into the green, he would keep them apart and let a thin band of dark paper sit between them, like the horizon at dusk. He painted the bottom half red, careful not to cross the line, then measured the top half against the bottom so the two sections stayed proportional. When he set the poster flat to dry, the colors glowed beside each other, clean and bright, no brown anywhere.

Mr. Doyle stopped on his way past with an armload of returned books. He looked at the sunset for a long moment. "Now that," he said, "is going to make people show up on Sunday."

"Two o'clock," Justin told him. "Audition's at two."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
Nicholas had promised Mr. Fitzgerald the corrected homework by tomorrow morning, and he was not going to be negligent about it twice. He spread his math sheet on the kitchen table next to his science folder, where a slide of pond water sat waiting under his grandfather's old microscope. He wanted to look for a microbe before dinner, but the math came first, so he pulled his chair close and grabbed a pencil.

The problem stared back at him: 2x + 3x + 7 = 22. Easy, he thought, and he wrote 5x + 7 = 22 in one quick motion. He was on fire. Then the next one: 2x + 3 = 11. He wrote 5x = 8, and something in his stomach went cold.

"Grandma, is this right?" he asked. His grandmother, a retired teacher, was peeling an orange at the counter, and Lucian, who had come over to build a model rocket, looked up from the glue.

She leaned over the page. "In the first one you condensed 2x and 3x into 5x. In the second, tell me, what does the x stand for?"

"Stands for... the mystery number," Nicholas said slowly.

"So 2x is two mystery numbers," she said, tapping the paper, "and 3 is just plain 3. Can you condense those?"

Nicholas stared. Two mystery numbers plus three ordinary ones. You couldn't squash them together. Like trying to add the rocket parts and the glue into one pile. "No," he said. "2x and 3 can't combine, because one has a variable and one doesn't. Only like terms go together. So 2x stays 2x, and I subtract 3 from both sides. 2x = 8. Then x = 4."

"Check it," his grandmother said.

"Two times 4 is 8, plus 3 is 11." He threw his pencil in the air and caught it. "It works! Grandma, it actually works!"

Lucian bounded over, nearly knocking the slide. "Forget math, look at the rocket. If I get the fins glued before dinner, we can launch Saturday and beat Erica's height record. She got twelve feet last week."

Nicholas was already halfway to the microscope. "One microbe, one minute, then fins." He pressed his eye to the lens and there it was, a tiny thing spinning through the green water. He let Lucian look too, and while his friend shouted at the speck, Nicholas scribbled one last problem on a scrap of paper and handed it to his grandmother.

"Make one for me," he said. "A hard one."

She wrote 4x + 2 + x = 17 and slid it across. Nicholas grinned, but then he stopped. "Wait. Did you just make that up, or does it come out even?"

She smiled and went back to her orange. "Solve it and see."

"5x + 2 = 17," he said aloud, pencil flying. "5x = 15. x = 3. Grandma, you couldn't fool me if you tried."

"Saturday," Lucian said, holding up a fin. "Twelve feet and one inch. Minimum."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
The folded paper from the eye doctor had been burning a hole in Maeva's backpack all morning, and by third period she could not stand it anymore. She smoothed it out on her desk and read the typed line again: -2.00. A negative number. Her eyes, apparently, had gotten a score worse than zero.

"Psst," she whispered to Emelia, who sat one row over. "Did your eye doctor give you a number too?" Emelia dug through her binder and produced her own slip. "+1.50," it said, plain as anything. Positive. Maeva's stomach dropped. So other people got plus signs, and she got a minus? She turned to Franklin next, but Franklin had perfect vision and rolled his eyes at the very question.

After class, Ms. Wiśniewski was erasing the board, and Maeva lingered by her desk with both slips held out like evidence. "Is mine bad? It says negative two." She waited for the bad news. Would she have to wear the glasses forever? Her dad wore glasses, and his dad before him, so maybe the whole thing was hereditary, passed down like the crooked nose in their family photos.

Ms. Wiśniewski did not sigh or lecture. She only asked, "What does yours say again? And Emelia's?" She tapped the numbers with one finger, the way she did when she wanted students to find an answer themselves.

Maeva looked. Her minus. Emelia's plus. Emelia squinted when she read, holding pages at arm's length, while Maeva could never see the board without the front row. Two different problems, two different signs. "The minus is mine," Maeva said slowly, "because I can't see far. And the plus is hers because she can't see close. They're opposites." She checked it against everything she knew, and it held.

"And the number itself," Ms. Wiśniewski said, "measures lens strength. They call it diopters."

"Diopters," Maeva repeated, and then she could not help grinning. Nothing about her eyes was below zero. There was no bad score at all. There was only a system, and she had cracked it. On the way out, she and Emelia reached a settlement: Emelia would disclose the location of her secret candy stash in exchange for Maeva's seat in the front row, which Emelia suddenly claimed she'd always wanted.

At lunch, Maeva put on the new glasses for the first time and looked across the cafeteria. "Franklin!" she shouted. "You have a zit on your forehead!"

"Rude," said Franklin.

"Amazing," said Maeva, and counted the ceiling tiles, far away, one by one.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
Avery laid the sleeping bag across her bed like a body and stared at the packing list until the words blurred. Camp Kanawa, two weeks, her first time anywhere without her mom. She had a theory that if she packed perfectly, everything else would go perfectly too, which was obviously not how the world worked, but the theory gave her motivation anyway.

The doorbell rang and Alaric came in holding his phone. "Giuliano sent you the photo, right?" he asked. "From last year. His shoulders." Avery had seen it. Giuliano had gone to the same camp, spent one long afternoon at the lake, and come home the color of a cooked lobster. "He told me he put on sunscreen that morning," Alaric said. "Full coverage. His mom watched him do it."

Avery sat down on the sleeping bag, pushing the packing list aside. "Then how did he burn?" Something had to be hidden here, a cause she couldn't see from the photo. Giuliano had done the right thing at the start and still ended up wrecked. She remembered Giuliano's messages from that week: swim practice in the morning, the scavenger hunt on the beach, the soccer game on the sand courts, all of it outside, all of it in one afternoon. She went back through the chat, scrolling slowly. "Alaric. When did he put it on?" "Like seven a.m. He said so." "And the lake afternoon went until four." She let out a long breath, almost an inhale of realization. "It wears off. It has to. Nobody said anything about putting it on again."

They tested the idea the only way they could. Avery texted Giuliano directly: did anyone at camp ever reapply, or did everyone treat the morning application as a one-time deal? His answer came in three minutes. "Nobody mentioned it. The counselors assumed we knew. My mom was furious when the nurse said it." Then a second message: "Reapply about every two hours outdoors. And right after swimming or sweating hard, because it washes and rubs off." Avery read it twice. Nine hours at the lake with one application at dawn. The math did the rest.

She didn't pack one bottle. She packed three travel sizes and a zippered pouch for the lake bag, and she wrote herself a note in capitals on a sticky label: TWO HOURS. AFTER SWIMMING. Alaric watched her tape it inside her daypack. "You know the counselors will have some," he said. "Probably." "Then I'll have my own," Avery said. "I want to look like someone who thought of this already." She folded a sun hat on top of the sleeping bag and zipped the duffel shut in one pull.
